title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

context_blocks.text: A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.

importance.reason: A defining computational learning problem originating with the PAC framework, explicitly highlighted in successive surveys and connected to representation-independent learning hardness, decision-tree learning and junta learning. Selected for the Learning theory focus prefix after correcting the mislabelled junta record; the score reflects breadth and foundational significance, not the date of this review.

progress.text: Feldman explicitly states the original arbitrary-distribution random-example question before discussing restricted distributions and query models.
Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz prove improper-learning hardness conditional on random-K-SAT refutation hardness.
Daniely–Vardi derive improper-learning hardness for superconstant term bounds from a local-PRG assumption.
Alman and coauthors post faster exact learning with membership and equivalence queries; these remain extra forms of access.
Servedio’s survey retains the general gap and distinguishes the distribution-free upper bound from uniform-input learning.
The relative-error DNF testing preprint studies a different output and query model.
Iterative Chow Filtering provides quasipolynomial-time uniform-training DNF guarantees in the PQ model.

sentences: A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of possibly negated Boolean variables, with the number of terms bounded by the supplied size parameter.

The learner sees only independent noiseless labeled examples from an arbitrary unknown distribution and must run in one polynomial in dimension, term bound and the stated accuracy/confidence parameters.
Its output may be any explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit whose predictions have small distributional error with high probability.

Polynomial sample complexity is available, while known improper-learning lower bounds remain conditional and recent positive results use restricted distributions, stronger query access or different output guarantees.
A solution needs a complete Lean proof of the full uniform learner guarantee or a negation covering every allowed learner and polynomial bound.

source_formulation.text: The inherited question comes from the first paragraph of Feldman’s 2012 introduction: polynomial-time PAC learning of polynomial-size DNFs from random examples under an arbitrary unknown distribution. The retained size-sensitive statement permits improper learning. The integer learning parameters, explicit circuit syntax and charged example-access convention specify that target rather than adding query access or restricting the hypothesis to DNF.

checked_sources: Downloaded Feldman COLT 2012 full PDF and read abstract and Section 1. Its first paragraph poses learning polynomial-size DNFs from random examples under an arbitrary unknown distribution; later positive results have product/uniform/smoothed or membership-query conditions.

Checked arXiv:2511.08791 current history: version 1, November 11, 2025. Downloaded the full survey and read Section 2.2 model/hypothesis discussion, the accuracy/confidence and finite-class sample discussions, Theorem 8 with the general 2^(tilde O(n^(1/3) log s)) bound, and Theorem 13 for uniform-input random examples. The survey deliberately suppresses learning-parameter dependence in its general complexity display. No derivation or solver recipe is retained in the card.

Downloaded the Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz COLT 2016 paper. Read Assumption 1 (random K-SAT refutation at n^f(K) clauses with f growing), Terminology 2, Theorem 3, Corollary 4 and Section 2.1. The theorem covers improper learning but relies on the specified unproved refutation hypothesis; it is not a consequence of bare P != NP asserted here.

Downloaded Daniely–Vardi COLT 2021. Read Assumption 1, its polynomial-stretch/constant-advantage interpretation, Section 2.3 and Theorem 3. The DNF theorem uses Assumption 1 and permits any efficiently evaluable hypothesis. The separate Assumption 2 is not substituted, and a lower bound restricted to proper DNF output would not meet this card’s target.

Checked arXiv:2605.17251v1 dated May 17, 2026, with no later revision listed. Downloaded full PDF and read abstract, Definition 1.1 PQ model, Definition 1.2 and Theorem 1.1. The DNF application has uniform training marginal, quasipolynomial time and selective predictions with rejection control; it does not establish polynomial-time ordinary distribution-free PAC learning.

Current author-page and arXiv checks identify Alman et al. arXiv:2507.20336v1, July 27, 2025, as the faster exact learner also described in an April 2026 talk. Primary abstracts confirm membership and equivalence queries; the talk date is not treated as a new paper date. The full proof was not retrieved. The separate STOC 2025 Locally Mixing Random Walks author abstract was also read: its quasipolynomial learner uses membership queries and an equal-term-size promise, while its general result lists a single target term.

Read primary author/arXiv abstracts and current history for Chen–Pires–Pitassi–Servedio arXiv:2601.16076v1, January 22, 2026. This is relative-error function property testing with query access. An author listing for FOCS 2026 is not represented as a verified publication date or a full proof review.
